paper_title: Steering Black-Box Large Language Model Agents with Pitfall Anticipation World Model

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Frontier black-box Large Language Model (LLM) agents are proficient at long-horizon reasoning and precise action generation. However, when it comes to a specific agentic task, they have no internalized knowledge of how that particular environment unfolds. A world model offers a natural remedy, providing the agent with environment specific knowledge by foreseeing how the environment will respond to the action it is about to take. Prior world models for LLM agents mainly predict next observations at each step, which is costly and often uninformative because individual observations provide limited task-relevant guidance and not every step requires call for foresight. This raises a key question: what a world model should predict and when should it be invoked for agentic tasks? Our pilot study suggests that world model guidance is most useful when it anticipates pitfalls within a bounded multi-step future. Motivated by this, we introduce Pitfall Anticipation World Model (PAWM), which selectively intervenes when a potential pitfall arises and predicts the impending failure to steer the agent away from it. PAWM is trained in two stages: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) on synthetic data labeled with agent pitfalls, followed by GRPO co-training with a black-box LLM to further optimize it in the target environment. PAWM improves Claude Sonnet 4.5 performance by 24.3% on ScienceWorld and 7.7% on WebArena-Lite, outperforming a range of baselines. These results demonstrate that PAWM provides an effective form of world model guidance for black-box LLM agents.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Frontier LLMs such as GPT-5 and Claude are increasingly deployed in customized agentic applications (Yao et al., 2023), from enterprise workflow automation (Yao et al., 2024; Barres et al., 2025) to specialized domain assistants (Trivedi et al., 2024; *Work was done during an internship at AWS AI. 1 Jimenez et al., 2024). Owing to large-scale training, these models already excel at the core competencies such as instruction following, general reasoning, task planning, long contexts processing, and producing precise, well-formatted actions via function calling or code. What they still lack is not general capability but task-specific reliability for agents. Since these models are black-box, such reliability cannot be instilled by fine-tuning their weights. This has inspired growing interest in steering black-box LLM agents (Li et al., 2024; Asawa et al., 2025; Lingam et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026a), where an external module injects guidance that shapes the frozen models behavior at inference time. However, prior steering methods mainly focus on assisting agent planning, such as decomposing the goal into subgoals or laying out high-level action sequences. Advising black-box LLM agents on it reinforces capabilities they already possess, rather than providing the environment knowledge they lack about how specific agentic environment responds to their actions. We therefore propose to steer black-box LLM agents with world models (Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018; Li et al., 2026), which can supply this missing environment knowledge. Rather than encoding what to do, world model captures how the environment behaves, how states transit in response to actions, and how task trajectory is likely to unfold. black-box LLM, although capable in general, has never internalized such environment-specific dynamics for the agent task at hand. This makes the world model natural approach for supplying black-box LLM agents with the grounding they lack. growing body of work has begun to explore LLM-based world models for agentic tasks, using them to foresee future states and thereby guide action selection. Most of these works, however, employ the world model as simulator of the environment that rolls out actions to the next observations to support candidates ranking or tree-based search (Zhao et al., 2023; Gu et al., Figure 1: Illustration for Pitfall Anticipation World Model in steering black-box LLM agents. 2024; Chae et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2026; Guan et al., 2026). Whether using world model as direct source of additional environment knowledge in the agent loop helpful or not remains unclear. For instance, Qian et al. (2026) found that generative world model provides no consistent benefit for agents, whether invoked adaptively or at every step, with performance sometimes even worse than when acting without world model. Therefore, how to effectively deliver world models guidance remains an open problem. Two design decisions are central here, and prior work has left both implicit. First, what should the world model output? Environment knowledge can be surfaced at very different granularities, from the immediate consequence of the current step to summary of the entire remaining trajectory, and it is not obvious which is most useful to frozen agent. Second, when should the world model intervene? Guiding at every step supplies the most information but risks overwhelming or misdirecting an already-capable agent, whereas intervening too rarely risks staying silent at the steps that matter. Neither question has settled answer, and together they define the design space for this work. To answer these questions, we first conduct systematic pilot study on the ScienceWorld (Wang et al., 2022) and WebArena-Lite (Zhou et al., 2024) benchmarks, in each case training world model via SFT on collected agent trajectories to steer Claude Sonnet 4.5 agent model. Along the world model output axis, we compare guidance of increasing horizon: the next observation alone, the segment up to the next subgoal, and the entire remaining trajectory. Our experiment results reveal that guidance bounded at the next subgoal works best, indicating that world model should look several steps ahead yet stop at meaningful boundary. Along the intervention axis, we start from the observation that most guidance leaves the agents action unchanged, and ask what distinguishes the guidance that does change it. Both lexical and an LLM-based semantic analysis show that pitfall-related generations dominate the guidance that changes the agents action. To verify that anticipated pitfalls indeed make good timing for intervention, we run gating ablation that routes only pitfall-anticipating guidance to the agent, and find that it nearly matches guiding at every step in performance with far less cost. These studies point to two design principles: guidance is most useful when it forecasts multi-step future bounded at meaningful milestone, and its value concentrates at potential pitfalls. Inspired by our pilot study, we propose Pitfall Anticipatory World Model (PAWM), world model that steers black-box LLM agent by anticipating pitfalls only when they are likely to arise. Unlike prior world models that simulate candidate actions or provide guidance at every step, PAWM stays silent while the agent is on promising trajectory and intervenes only when it foresees an impending failure, at which point it predicts the pitfall ahead and issues multi-step forward-looking guidance that steers the agent away from the action it is about to take. By stepping in only at these key moments, PAWM avoids unnecessary guidance and acts exactly where the agent would otherwise fail, making it both more efficient and effective. We obtain PAWM in two stages. First, we perform SFT on synthetic pitfall dataset in which separate LLM annotates repeatedly sampled trajectories, contrasting successful and failed run of the same task to locate the key pitfall steps and describing the corresponding failure risks. This teaches PAWM both to foresee potential pitfalls and to articulate the guidance needed to avoid them. Furthermore, to optimize the anticipation ability for the agents downstream task success, we apply GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) to co-train PAWM with the frozen black-box model, adapting its steering to the specific agent and environment. Integrating PAWM with Claude Sonnet 4.5 agent yields success rates of 78.9% on ScienceWorld and 80.4% on WebArena-Lite, significantly outperforming the black-box Sonnet agent, which reaches only 54.6% In addition, compared and 72.7% respectively. with range of baselines, including steering blackbox LLM agents with pre-task guidance and world models under various settings, PAWM consistently performs best, demonstrating its effectiveness of steering agents with environment-specific pitfall knowledge.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Steering Black-box LLMs. Frontier LLMs are often accessible only through APIs, making taskspecific parameter updates infeasible. Prior work therefore adapts these models externally, either through prompt optimization (Shin et al., 2020; Fernando et al., 2024) or by training auxiliary models that provide input-dependent guidance while keeping the underlying LLM fixed (Li et al., 2023). Recent work extends this paradigm to complex agentic tasks, where lightweight advisors provide high-level guidance to steer the behavior of blackbox LLM agents (Li et al., 2024; Asawa et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026a). World Models. World models learn environment dynamics to support planning and decisionmaking (Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018; Hafner et al., 2019b,a). For LLM agents, they are commonly used to generate synthetic experience (Gao et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025; Ding et al., 2026), internalize environment dynamics into agents (Zhang et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2025, 2026b), or assist action selection through simulation and search (Zhao et al., 2023; Gu et al., 2024; Chae et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2026; Guan et al., 2026). Our setting instead considers world model that continuously assists black-box LLM in the agent loop. Although recent work explores similar interaction patterns (Qian et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026), they offer no systematic study of how world model should help the agent. Additional discussion of related works is provided in Appendix A.

sections.title: 3 Pilot Study
sections.content: Before developing our method, we conduct pilot study to systematically explore the design space introduced above: what world model should output and when it should intervene. All experiments use Claude Sonnet 4.5 as fixed black-box agent, guided by separately trained world model with the base Qwen3.5-27B, ensuring that any performance differences arise from the world models guidance rather than changes to the agent itself.

sections.title: 3.1 Problem Definition and Experiment Setup
sections.content: We formalize the agent task as Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP) = (S, A, O, , R), where denotes the environment state space, the action space, the observation space, the transition dynamics, and the reward function. Given task Q, the agent does not directly observe the underlying environment state and instead acts based on its interaction history ht = (q, o1, a1, . . . , at1, ot) at step t, where ot and at denote the observation received and the action taken at step t, respectively. The agent here is frozen black-box policy π that can only be queried but not be updated. Our goal is to learn world model ωθ that improves the agents performance without modifying π. Concretely, at each step, the agent first proposes tentative action at π(ht). Rather than executing it immediately, the world model rolls the action forward and produces guidance gt ωθ(ht, at) that anticipates its consequences. The resulting guidance is then appended to the agents context, allowing the agent to repropose the action as at π(ht, at, gt), either retaining the tentative action or revising it in light of the predicted outcome. Finally, only at is executed, yielding the next observation ot+1, after which the process repeats. In this way, the world model steers the agent through πs own context rather than selecting actions or searching on its behalf. Note that both the agent and the world model operate turn-wise: at each step, they are queried 3 with the interaction history ht reconstructed from scratch rather than accumulated through the agents message list. We adopt this design for two reasons. First, raw observations can be lengthy, such as full HTML page in WebArena-Lite. Reconstructing ht allows us to compress past observations, keeping the context manageable over long horizons. Second, when rebuilding the context, we omit previous world model guidance to prevent its influence from carrying over to subsequent decisions. Prompts used to implement this turn-wise agent are provided in Appendix B. We evaluate our approach on two benchmarks: ScienceWorld (Wang et al., 2022), text-based environment that demands long-horizon interactions and WebArena-Lite (Zhou et al., 2024), an online web-navigation environment with rich, dynamic observations. In both, Claude Sonnet 4.5 serves as the black-box LLM agent π and we obtain the world model ωθ by collecting agent trajectories, extracting the environment dynamics and then perform SFT on them with the base model Qwen3.5-27B.

sections.title: 3.2 What Should the World Model Output?
sections.content: We first vary the content of the world models output while keeping its intervention at every step, comparing guidance over increasingly longer horizons. Specifically, we consider the following output types. (1) Next observation (Next-Obv): the world model predicts only the immediate observation resulting from the tentative action at. (2) Future trajectory: the world model instead summarizes the upcoming trajectory at two different horizons: the segment leading to the next subgoal (SubGoal-Traj), and the entire remaining trajectory to task completion (Full-Traj). These output types differ only in how their training targets are constructed. Starting from the same set of collected agent trajectories, we prompt an LLM to generate the corresponding target for each output type, yielding one dataset variant per setting. All variants are then trained under the same SFT setup, with details provided in Appendix C.1. We report Task Success Accuracy (Acc) averaged over three runs, together with the average Action Change Rate (ACR), defined as the fraction of guided steps at which the agent revises its tentative action at, to quantify how strongly the world models output affects the agent. N/A denotes the baseline without world model. Table 1 summarizes the results and reveals several clear trends. First, predicting only the next observation is weak steering signal, yielding WM Output N/A Next-Obv Full-Traj SubGoal-Traj ScienceWorld WebArena-Lite Acc 54.6 58.5 65.6 66.7 ACR 20.1 19.4 18.2 Acc 72.7 73.1 71.1 74.1 ACR 15.9 24.6 17.7 Table 1: Acc(%) and ACR(%) of frozen agent guided by world models with various outputs. marginal gains over the baseline without world models. This may be because single step rarely reveals enough information to advise the agent. Besides, extending the forecast to the entire remaining trajectory does not solve this and even falls below the baseline on WebArena-Lite, where long-horizon prediction may accumulate error and disrupt an agent that was already on track. The SubGoal-Traj variant performs best on both benchmarks, indicating that the value of world model lies in multi-step forward-looking bounded at meaningful milestone. Furthermore, Next-Obv on ScienceWorld and Full-Traj on WebArena-Lite attain the highest ACR yet the lowest Acc, showing that frequently revising the agents tentative action does not ensure improved task accuracy.

sections.title: 3.3 When Should the World Model Intervene?
sections.content: As shown in Table 1, most world model interventions do not alter the agents tentative actions. This motivates us to avoid intervening at every step, which is both costly and potentially disrupts an already capable agent. To understand when world model guidance actually matters, we contrast the world model generations that do change the tentative action (CHANGED) against those leave it unchanged (UNCHANGED). Lexical Analysis. We first perform lexical analysis of which words distinguish the two groups. Since raw frequency is dominated by generic words, we rank words by the weighted log-odds ratio with uninformative Dirichlet prior (Monroe et al., 2008), which contrasts words frequency in the CHANGED and UNCHANGED groups, then standardizes it into z-score so that rare terms are down-weighted. To surface environment-invariant terms, we compute this z-score separately per benchmark and rank words by the minimum of the two, zw min, which requires word to be distinctive in both environments. higher zw min therefore means that the word is over-represented in CHANGED group on both benchmarks. Formulations to compute zw min are given in Appendix C.2. 4 As shown in Table 2, the most distinctive words are associated with anticipated failure or stagnation, including explicit negative outcomes such as fails and without, predictions of an unchanged state such as remains, and contrastive markers such as however that signal mismatch between the intended and predicted outcomes. This suggests that the agent change its action mainly when the world model anticipates that the tentative action would lead to failures or no progress. Refer to Appendix C.2 for additional top-k words and word cloud visualizations. Semantic Analysis. Lexical statistics capture word-level patterns but not their semantic meaning, so we complement this analysis by prompting an LLM (Claude Sonnet 4.5) to make binary judgment for each world model guidance: whether it anticipates pitfall, i.e., warns that the tentative action will fail, stall, or not achieve the goal. We apply this classifier to 400 guidance generations randomly sampled from each group and pooled across both benchmarks. The detailed classifier prompt is provided in Appendix C.3. Results show that pitfall anticipations account for 76.8% of the CHANGED group but only 29.0% of the UNCHANGED group, statistically significant difference (χ2 = 181.1, df = 1, < 0.001). This semantic analysis reinforces the lexical evidence, showing that the agent is substantially more likely to revise its tentative action when the world model anticipates pitfalls. Gating Ablation. The analysis above shows that pitfall anticipation is associated with behavior change, but it remains unclear whether it can serve as criterion for deciding when world model guidance should intervene. To investigate this, we use an LLM classifier as gate on the SubGoal-Traj world model: the world model generates guidance at each step, but the gate determines whether that guidance is passed to the agent based on whether it anticipates pitfall. We compare three conditions: All, which passes every guidance; Pitfallonly, which passes guidance only when it anticipates pitfall; and Non-pitfall-only, which only passes the non-pitfall guidance. We additionally report Intervention Rate (IR), the fraction of steps at which guidance is actually passed to the agent, and #Calls, the average number of black-box agent queries per task. The gating prompt is provided in Appendix C.4. As shown in Table 3, Pitfall-only nearly matches All in agent performance while requiring substantially fewer black-box API calls, whereas Non-pitfall-only performs clearly worse despite intervening more often. The remaining gap between Pitfall-only and All is expected: the gate relies on post-hoc classifier, which may not filter out useful guidance, and the world model is also not explicitly optimized to produce pitfall anticipations that are most helpful for steering the agent. Nevertheless, these results suggest that pitfall anticipation provides promising criterion for when to intervene, retaining most benefit of the world model guidance at much lower cost.

sections.title: 4 Pitfall Anticipation World Models
sections.content: Inspired by the findings of our pilot study, we propose Pitfall Anticipation World Model (PAWM). PAWM is trainable world model that monitors frozen black-box LLM agent and, whenever it foresees an impending failure, describes the pitfall ahead and issues forward-looking guidance that steers the agent away from the action it was about to take. We first specify our PAWM and then describe the two stages that produce it: SFT on synthetic pitfall dataset and GRPO co-training with the black-box LLM agent.

sections.title: 4.1 PAWM Definition
sections.content: PAWM extends the world model of Section 3.1 with one key mechanism, where the output is gated. It emits special <pass> format output when the proposed action has no anticipated pitfall, in which case no guidance is injected and the agent simply 5 commits to at. Otherwise, it outputs the guidance gt, which is description of the impending failure and how to avoid it. Then, the agent reproposes the action as at π(ht, at, gt). The gate operationalizes the when principle, where intervention happens only at decisive steps. While the content of gt operationalizes the what, which is multi-step, forward-looking guidance concentrated at pitfalls.

sections.title: 4.2 Stage 1: SFT on Synthetic Pitfall Dataset
sections.content: The goal of the first stage is to teach PAWM where pitfalls may occur and how to warn against them. Trajectory collection. We first gather pool of agent trajectories by repeatedly running the blackbox LLM agent on the training set three times with 1.0 sampling temperature, retaining both successful and failed ones: failures localize where agents actually go wrong, while successes provide the contrastive correct continuation. Pitfall labeling. For each trajectory, we use separate LLM (Claude Sonnet 4.5) as an annotator to identify the key pitfall steps at which the task begins to fail. When both successful and failed trajectories are available for the same task, the annotator contrasts them to locate where the failed run diverges from the successful one. For each identified pitfall step, the LLM annotator then describes the potential pitfalls and provides corrective guidance to avoid it, which we denote as gt. All other steps are labeled <pass>. To improve sample utilization, we also handle tasks without mixture of successful and failed trajectories. For tasks with only successful trajectories, the annotator identifies residual pitfalls, such as suboptimal but non-fatal detours, so that successful runs do not degenerate into all-pass labels. For tasks with only failed trajectories, we rerun the agent with ground-truth guidance injected to obtain successful trajectories, and then contrast these guided successes against the original failures. In this way, tasks whose sampled trajectories are entirely successful or failed can still provide useful pitfall supervision rather than being discarded. Because the annotator labels trajectories in hindsight, it may leak future knowledge that PAWM has no way of accessing when deployed. To avoid this, we constrain the LLM annotator to describe each pitfall in general, abstracted terms grounded in what the agent has observed up to that step. This yields dataset = {(ht, at, gt)}, pairing each history and tentative action with the target guidance. Refer to Appendix for prompt details. Training objective. We fine-tune ωθ by minimizing the negative log-likelihood loss on D: LSFT(θ) = E(ht,at,gt)D (cid:2) log ωθ(gtht, at)(cid:3) Since the majority of steps are labeled <pass>, and training on this natural distribution biases ωθ toward always passing and rarely issuing guidance. To counter this, we down-sample <pass> steps to an empirically selected <pass>-to-anticipation ratio detailed in Section 5.2.

sections.title: 5 Experiment
sections.content: In this section, we detail the experiments conducted to evaluate PAWM. Specifically, we outline the experimental setup, discuss the main results with additional ablation study.

sections.title: 5.1 Experimental Setup
sections.content: Datasets. We conduct experiments on two agentic dataset WebArena and ScienceWorld. WebArena comprises 812 tasks. Following Qi et al. (2025), we use 165 verified tasks for evaluation (also named WebArena-Lite) and the remaining 647 tasks as the training set. Since RL rollouts with WebArena issue write actions that mutate website state and can contaminate other tasks, we use WebServ (Lu et al., 2025), which leverages Incus containers to create an isolated container per task. Detailed RL environment settings of WebArena are shown in Appendix E. For ScienceWorld, it spans 30 task types, each with variations that ScienceWorld partitions into disjoint train/dev/test splits. We collect training data on the train split with up to 30 variations per task (708 tasks) and evaluate on the test split with up to 10 variations per task (271 tasks). Models. Unless otherwise noted, the black-box LLM for the agent is Claude Sonnet4.5, accessed through the Amazon Bedrock API only, and all world models are built on Qwen3.5-27B(Qwen Team, 2026) backbone. Training Details. To obtain PAWM, we first run SFT on the synthetic pitfall dataset and GRPO cotraining is then initialized from this checkpoint. Training details are presented in Appendix F. Evaluation Details. To reduce evaluation variance, we set the temperature of both the agent model and the world model to 0 during evaluation. Even so, non-determinism environment and minor variability in the LLM serving stack prevent fully reproducible generations. We therefore run every evaluation three times and report averaged results. For both datasets, we report the average Task Success Accuracy (Acc) with its standard deviation, as well as the Pass@3, where task is deemed solved if at least one of these three runs succeeds. Baseline Methods. We compare the PAWMsteered black-box LLM agent against various baselines. (1) N/A: the black-box LLM agent acts on its own without any external guidance. (2) RAG: an embedding model retrieves the most similar previously solved task, and its successful trajectory is inserted into the agents context as guidance. (3) Pre-Task Guidance: Qwen3.5-27B is trained to generate task-specific guidance conditioned on the task query, providing advice to the agent before it starts. (4) Next-Obv/Full-Traj/SubGoal-Traj WM: We also compare world model steering methods with different output contents. Implementation details for baselines are included in Appendix G.

sections.title: 5.2 Results
sections.content: We present our main results in Table 4, comparing PAWM against various baseline steering methods applied to the same black-box LLM agent Claude Sonnet 4.5. From the table, we can clearly observe that PAWM (+GRPO) performs best across both benchmarks and metrics, reaching 78.9% Acc on ScienceWorld and 80.4% on WebArena-Lite, improving over the unassisted agent (N/A) by 24.3% and 7.7%. We also observe that GRPO improves Acc far more than Pass@3. This suggests that the two stages play complementary roles, where SFT provides the environment knowledge that sets the ceiling reflected in Pass@3, and GRPO makes the agent realize it more reliably. For fair comparison, we also apply GRPO to the baseline steering methods on ScienceWorld, initialized from their SFT checkpoints, including PreTask Guidance and world model variants with different outputs. sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: This paper studies how to steer black-box LLM agents by providing the environment knowledge they lack with world models. Guided by pilot study on what world model should output and when it should intervene, we propose Pitfall Anticipation World Model (PAWM), which anticipates pitfalls for the agents only when they are likely to arise. PAWM is first trained by SFT on synthetic pitfall dataset, then co-trained with the frozen agent via GRPO to adapt to the specific environment. Our experiments show that Claude Sonnet 4.5 steered by PAWM outperforms various baselines, and its learned pitfall knowledge transfers across agent backbones, demonstrating that anticipating pitfalls is an effective way for world model to assist black-box LLM agents.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: Due to the accessibility and cost of repeatedly querying proprietary models, our experiments are primarily scoped to Claude Sonnet 4.5 as the blackbox LLM agent used for trajectory collection and GRPO co-training. Although the resulting PAWM transfers to several other agent backbones during evaluation, we do not independently co-train with each of them, so agent specific differences in optimal pitfall anticipation remain underexplored. Our study is also limited to ScienceWorld and WebArena-Lite, and the high cost of online interaction, particularly in WebArena-Lite, limits the scale of reinforcement learning experiments. In addition, the world models studied here are task-specific: they are trained on trajectories collected from particular agentic environment rather than as large-scale, general-purpose world models. Accordingly, our conclusions should be interpreted within this task-specific setting, and may not directly extend to broader world models trained across many environments or domains. Finally, PAWM relies on synthetic pitfall supervision generated by LLM hindsight annotations. Although we constrain the annotations to information available up to the current step, they may still contain noise or teacher-model bias, and our definition of pitfall may not capture all forms of suboptimal behavior.

sections.title: Ethical Considerations
sections.content: This work aims to improve the reliability of blackbox LLM agents through world model guidance. However, inaccurate guidance may lead to undesirable agent behavior, and the proposed method could potentially be misused to enhance agent capabilities in unintended applications. Our evaluation is limited to benchmark environments, and caution is warranted when deploying the method in real-world settings.

sections.title: A Related Works
sections.content: Steering Black-box LLMs. Frontier LLMs such as GPT-5 and Claude are often accessed only through APIs, making their weights unavailable for task-specific adaptation. One line of work adapts them through automatic prompt optimization, searching for fixed prompt that is reused across all inputs (Shin et al., 2020; Fernando et al., 2024). Such static prompts, however, cannot adapt to individual tasks. more flexible paradigm is to use separate model to provide adaptive guidance, an idea long explored in reinforcement learning through teacher-student action advising and policy transfer (Fachantidis et al., 2017; Deng et al., 2025). In the context of black-box LLMs, this idea has been instantiated by training smaller model that produces per-task guidance while leaving the target LLM untouched (Li et al., 2023). Recently, growing body of works extend this idea to agentic tasks, training lightweight advisor model to steer black-box LLM agent with pre-task highlevel guidance (Li et al., 2024; Asawa et al., 2025; Lingam et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026a). These advisor models, however, mostly supply agent planning or task decomposition, which still builds on the black-box models general reasoning ability rather than injecting knowledge it does not have. In contrast, we formulate our advisor as world model providing the environment-specific world knowledge that the agent model lacks. World Models. World models, which predict how an environment evolves in response to actions, were first developed for perception-rich control domains, where latent dynamics models are learned from visual observations and used for planning or policy learning (Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018; Hafner et al., 2019b,a). With the rise of LLM agents, this paradigm has naturally extended to text-based environments, where LLMs themselves can serve as world models by predicting future states or observations. Existing approaches differ primarily in how these world models are constructed and integrated into agent learning and decision-making. One line of work uses learned world model as source of synthetic experience: rather than collecting trajectories from the real environment, which can be costly or impractical, the agent rolls out the world model to generate training data (Gao et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025; Ding et al., 2026). Another line internalizes environment dynamics directly into the agent model, enabling it to reason about the anticipated consequences of its actions before execution (Zhang et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2025, 2026b). More recent work further explores jointly evolving the world model and the agent during training (Liu et al., 2026b,c). Our setting instead focuses on using world model to assist black-box LLM agent whose parameters cannot be fine-tuned. Prior approaches in this setting typically use the world model to simulate candidate actions and select the most promising one, or to support tree-based search over possible action sequences (Zhao et al., 2023; Gu et al., 2024; Chae et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2026; Guan et al., 2026). Such candidate-selection and search-based schemes can be computationally expensive, as the world model must be queried repeatedly across candidates and search branches, while most simulated trajectories are ultimately discarded. We instead consider an alternative paradigm in which the world model remains directly involved in the agent loop and provides guidance during execution, rather than serving only as simulator for ranking or pruning candidate actions. Although several recent works have begun to explore this form of world-model assistance (Qian et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026), they generally adopt fixed interaction pattern without systematically examining what information the world model should provide or when its guidance is most useful. Our work takes step toward addressing these questions. Prompts for Turn-wise Agent This section presents prompts used to realize the turn-wise agent on ScienceWorld and WebArena. Note that the world model only supplies additional guidance, injected at the point where the agent redecides on its tentative action, leaving the agents main process untouched. B.1 ScienceWorld The following shows the system and user prompts for the ScienceWorld agent. Text highlighted in red within braces marks placeholders that are filled with step-specific content at inference time. We also present the format of the agent history, which records the observations and actions from previous steps but excludes the valid action list, as repeating this long list for every past step would consume substantial context. At each step, ScienceWorld environment provides the agent with the current location, the room the agent is in and the objects 12 it contains with their states, the current inventory of objects the agent is carrying, the current observation returned by the environment for the last action, and the action list available at this step for the agent to choose from. Here we also specify the action reproposal prompt used for world model involved settings. Labels in square brackets, such as [Next-Obv], [Full-Traj], and [SubGoal-Traj], indicate the corresponding experimental setting and are not part of the actual prompt. The text following each label is the prompt content appended after the user prompt to ask the agent to reconsider its proposed action based on the world model guidance.

sections.title: System Prompt
sections.content: You are an agent playing ScienceWorld, textbased simulation of elementaryschool science experiments. You control character in house with rooms (kitchen, bathroom, workshop, greenhouse, etc.) that contain objects you can inspect and manipulate to complete scientific task. Rules: Each turn you receive the task, an AGENT HISTORY of your prior steps, your current location, your inventory, the result of your last action, and list of VALID ACTIONS you may take right now. You MUST choose exactly one action from the VALID ACTIONS list, copied verbatim. Do not invent objects or actions that are not listed. If the object you want (e.g. substance for "focus on X") is not in the list, it is not reachable from here yet move or inspect to bring it into view first, rather than naming it anyway. The list of valid actions changes each turn depending on where you are and what is nearby; move around and inspect objects to make more actions available. The VALID ACTIONS are shown compactly, grouped by verb to save space: * "open: doorA, doorB" means each object is separate action ("open doorA", "open doorB"). * "move to X: a, Y: c, d" is twoobject template: pick one item from and one from to form the action ("move to c"). Only combinations the game currently allows are valid. * line like "(connect ... electrical combos hidden)" means those actions exist but are omitted here because they are not needed for this task.

On EVERY step, respond in EXACTLY this twoline format and nothing else: Think: <your reasoning about the current state, what you have already tried (see AGENT HISTORY), and what to do next> Action: <a single action copied verbatim from the VALID ACTIONS list>

Consider this forecast, then decide using the current state above: if it changes your mind, pick different action; otherwise keep your PROPOSED ACTION and proceed. Respond in the required format with exactly one action. B.2 WebArena Similar to ScienceWorld, here we also list the system prompt, user prompt, agent history format and action reproposal prompt for WebArena Agent. In WebArena, the observation at each step is the current webpage. We parse its raw HTML into simplified format similar to an accessibility tree but keeping the semantic ID of each element, so that the agent can refer to elements directly in its actions. Since one single webpage is already long in context, the agent is required to summarize the current page and lay out its plan before producing an action, and it is this summary and plan, rather than the raw page, that is stored in the agent history as the compressed observation.

sections.title: C Experiment Details of Pilot Study
sections.content: This section provides additional experiment details in our pilot study. C.1 SFT Details for World Models Here we list the SFT details for training the world models with varied output contents in Section 3.2. SFT Dataset Construction. To collect the data for training these world models, we first sample trajectories on the training split of both datasets by running the baseline setting (N/A) with Claude Sonnet 4.5 as the agent, repeating each task three 16 times at generation temperature of 1.0. This results in 2,124 agent trajectories for ScienceWorld and 1,941 for WebArena. Since world model is meant to reflect the environments response to each action, failed trajectories remain useful, as they show how poor action leads to an unfavorable observation. We therefore split each collected trajectory at every time step and prompt Sonnet 4.5 to summarize the content that follows as the world models target output. The prompts used to generate targets for each setting are listed below. The agent future field follows the same format as the agent history, except that it covers the steps taken after the current one. Placeholders with multiple variants are listed at the end of each prompt box, where the tag in square brackets marks the condition and the text following it is the content substituted into the placeholder under that condition. For example, outcome is replaced with the [SUCCESS] line when the collected trajectory succeeded and with the [FAILURE] line when it failed. For Next-Obv on WebArena-Lite, no additional summarization is needed, as the agent already summarizes each page it sees as part of its output, so the summary produced at step + 1 serves directly as the target next observation. System Prompt for Next-Obv WM Targets Generation on ScienceWorld You are labeling training data for ScienceWorld NEXTOBSERVATION world model. separate "actor" agent plays the game; at some step it PROPOSED an action, and the game then transitioned to new state. Your job is to rewrite that ACTUAL RESULTING STATE into concise, naturallanguage PREDICTION of what the actor will be looking at right after the action executes the target world model should learn to produce from the state and the proposed action ALONE. You are given the TASK, the AGENT HISTORY, the CURRENT STATE the actor saw before acting, the PROPOSED NEXT ACTION, and as ground truth for labeling only the ACTUAL RESULTING STATE the game transitioned to. That resulting state has THREE parts, all after the action executed: the RESULT OBSERVATION (the game's text response), the RESULTING LOCATION (the room the actor is now in and what it contains), and the RESULTING INVENTORY (what the actor is now carrying). Summarize the WHOLE resulting state not just the terse result line into the world model's spoken prediction. ABOUT SCIENCEWORLD (so your summary is faithful): It is text simulation of elementaryschool science experiments. The actor moves between rooms and manipulates objects to complete scientific task. Common actions: move/teleport, open/close, pick up / put down / move objects, activate/deactivate devices (stove, freezer, blast furnace, sink), use thermometer, mix, read, wait (let time pass so heating/cooling/growth happens), and "focus on X" (a onetime, irreversible commitment marking the task target). The resulting state is the combination of: the game's terse text response (RESULT OBSERVATION), plus how the world now looks (RESULTING LOCATION the current room, its objects, open/closed doors, devices on/off) and what is held (RESULTING INVENTORY). single action can change any of these: entering new room, an object moving into/out of the inventory, device turning on, thermometer reading, container's contents, door opening, "focus" ending the episode, or "No known action"/no change. HOW TO WRITE THE PREDICTION: Describe the SINGLE resulting state one step from now not the end of the task. Do not forecast multiple steps ahead. Cover the WHOLE state transition, drawing on all three parts: what the game reported (result observation), WHERE the actor now is if it changed (resulting location), and WHAT it is now carrying if it changed (resulting inventory). Weave them into one coherent prediction rather than listing them as separate fields. Be FAITHFUL to the ACTUAL RESULTING STATE: report what actually happened, including "bad" outcome (no change, an invalid action, mislabeled target, device that did nothing because precondition was unmet, or "focus" ending the episode). Never sugarcoat it into the outcome the actor hoped for truthful prediction of bad next state is exactly the signal the world model must learn. Preserve TASKRELEVANT DETAILS verbatim: measurement readings and units (e.g. "35 degrees"), exact object/substance names, on/off and open/closed states, which room the actor moved to, what entered or left the inventory, and whether the episode ended. Keep numbers and names characterexact. FOCUS ON WHAT MATTERS FOR THE TASK: summarize the parts of the resulting state relevant to making progress (or the failure), and drop irrelevant scenery. couple of sentences is ideal; do not pad, and do not restate the entire room objectlist unless it changed in way that matters to the task. Write it as PREDICTION in the second person ("You ..."), the voice world model uses when telling the actor where its action lands. Do NOT mention that you were shown the actual result, and do NOT reference "ground truth" or "the label". Do NOT output literal actions, object IDs, or code. Plain natural language only. OUTPUT FORMAT: Output ONLY the predicted next observation, wrapped in <anticipation> and </anticipation> tags. Nothing else. For example: <anticipation>You are now in the kitchen holding the metal pot, but it is still empty: the sink was never turned on, so pouring did nothing and nothing entered the pot. The room is unchanged and you would need to activate the sink before any water is available.</anticipation> User Prompt for Next-Obv WM Targets Generation on ScienceWorld TASK: {task instruction} AGENT HISTORY (prior thoughts, actions, and short observations): {agent history} CURRENT STATE (room, inventory, last observation what the actor saw BEFORE acting): {current state} PROPOSED NEXT ACTION (the actor executed this): {proposed next action} ACTUAL RESULTING STATE (ground truth the whole state AFTER the action; label ONLY, the world model does not see this): RESULT OBSERVATION (the game's response to the action): {result observation} RESULTING LOCATION (the room after the action): {result location} or '(unchanged/unknown)' RESULTING INVENTORY (what you are carrying after the action): {result inventory} or '(unchanged/unknown)' Summarize this WHOLE ACTUAL RESULTING STATE the result observation together with the resulting location and inventory into the concise, taskfocused, secondperson PREDICTED NEXT OBSERVATION as specified. Output ONLY the <anticipation>...</anticipation> block. System Prompt for Full-Traj & SubGoal-Traj WM Targets Generation on ScienceWorld You are labeling training data for ScienceWorld TRAJECTORY world model. separate "actor" agent plays the game; at some step it PROPOSED an action, and the run then went on to unfold in particular way. Your job is to rewrite the AGENT FUTURE the steps the run ACTUALLY took from that point into concise, forwardlooking PREDICTION of the trajectory that the proposed action sets in motion. You are given the TASK, the AGENT HISTORY (the actor's prior steps and the state it currently faces), the AGENT FUTURE (ground truth the actions the run actually took from here and the states they produced), and the RUN OUTCOME (whether the run ultimately SUCCEEDED or FAILED). Turn that groundtruth future into the world model's spoken forecast the target it should learn to produce from the state and the proposed action ALONE. ABOUT SCIENCEWORLD (so your forecast is faithful): It is text simulation of elementaryschool science experiments. The actor moves between rooms and manipulates objects to complete scientific task. Common actions: move/teleport, open/close, pick up / put down / move objects, activate/deactivate devices (stove, freezer, blast furnace, sink), use thermometer, mix, read, wait (let time pass so heating/cooling/growth happens), and "focus on X" (a onetime, irreversible commitment marking the task target). State changes take TIME and PRECONDITIONS: heating/cooling require the substance on an active device and repeated waiting; containers must be open; substance must be identified and in hand before focusing. `focus on` the wrong object, or before the correct target is ready, usually FAILS the task with large penalty and ends the episode. HOW TO WRITE THE FORECAST: Trace the ARC of the trajectory the AGENT FUTURE shows the sequence of actions and the states they produce as coherent path, NOT perstep transcript. few sentences that convey where the path goes and how it ends (within the horizon you are told to stop at). Be FAITHFUL TO THE RUN OUTCOME. If the run SUCCEEDED, forecast the path reaching the 17 goal. If it FAILED, forecast the failure HONESTLY the wrong focus, the wasted loop, the missing precondition, the stall, the wrong/early termination. NEVER pretend failing run succeeds; truthful forecast of bad trajectory is exactly what lets the actor reconsider. Ground it in what the AGENT FUTURE actually contains. Do not invent steps that did not happen. Predictions grow less certain further out, so keep the later stretch appropriately tentative in wording, but stay faithful to the recorded future. Preserve TASKRELEVANT DETAILS: the correct/incorrect target focused on, key state changes (a device turned on, substance reaching temperature or changing state), and whether the episode ends. Keep object/substance names and numeric readings characterexact when they matter. Write it as PREDICTION in the second person ("You ..."), the voice world model uses when telling the actor where its action leads. Do NOT mention that you were shown the actual future, the run outcome label, or "ground truth". Do NOT output literal actions, object IDs, or code, and do NOT number the steps. Plain naturallanguage prose. OUTPUT FORMAT: Output ONLY the forecast, wrapped in <summary> and </summary> tags. Nothing else. For example: <summary>You move the metal pot with the water onto the stove, turn the stove on, and wait repeatedly as the temperature climbs; the water reaches its boiling point and changes to steam, and once you focus on the correct substance the task completes successfully.</summary> User Prompt for Full-Traj & SubGoal-Traj WM Targets Generation on ScienceWorld TASK: {task instruction} AGENT HISTORY (the actor's prior steps and the state it currently faces): {agent history} CURRENT STATE (room, inventory, last observation what the actor sees now): {current state} AGENT FUTURE (starting from the actor's decision at the current step, the steps this run ACTUALLY took ground truth, not guess): {agent future} RUN OUTCOME: this trajectory ultimately {outcome}. {summary instruction} Summarize it as coherent forwardlooking anticipation in the second person, faithful to the RUN OUTCOME (if it failed, forecast the failure honestly; do not pretend it succeeds). Wrap your final summary inside <summary> and </summary> tags. ================================================ NOTE (not part of the prompt): the placeholders below are each instantiated as one of the listed variants. ================================================ {outcome} [SUCCESS] SUCCEEDED it reached the goal and the task was scored complete [FAILURE] FAILED it did not complete the task correctly {summary instruction} [FullTraj] Summarize the AGENT FUTURE all the way to how the task TERMINATES (the actor's final action and whether it ends in success or failure). [SubGoalTraj] Summarize the AGENT FUTURE only UP TO THE NEXT MILESTONE the next key step of progress toward the task goal (reaching the right room, getting the correct substance/object in hand, device turned on with the target inside, the substance reaching the required temperature or state, or focusing on the correct target). Stop once that milestone is reached, or once the attempt to reach it clearly fails; do not summarize past it. Do not name the milestone explicitly just describe the path up to that stopping point. System Prompt for Full-Traj & SubGoal-Traj WM Targets Generation on WebArena You are an expert annotator who writes worldmodel summaries of how webnavigation task unfolds. separate "actor" agent drives the browser; your job is to summarize its future, not to take actions yourself. ABOUT THE ACTOR (a black box to you): The actor is an autonomous web agent that completes the objective by calling single tool, `step_browser`, once per turn. Each call performs one browser action and returns the resulting page state. `step_browser` can: click an element, type text into field (optionally pressing Enter), hover, select dropdown value, clear field, press key, navigate to URL, go back/forward, refresh, open/switch/close browser tab, and finally terminate the task while reporting an answer. Each turn the actor records an OBSERVATION SUMMARIZATION (what it observed that turn), PLANNING (its reasoning), and the ACTION it then took. One turn's action produces the next turn's observation. One step = one action together with the page it produces. WHAT YOU ARE GIVEN: The TASK OBJECTIVE. The AGENT HISTORY: the steps the actor has already taken up to the current state. The AGENT FUTURE: the remaining steps this run ACTUALLY took (GROUND TRUTH, not guess), possibly truncated to horizon you are told about below. Each future step shows the observation the actor saw, its planning, and the action it took. The RUN OUTCOME: whether this run ultimately SUCCEEDED or FAILED. This is the real outcome of the trajectory you are summarizing. YOUR JOB: Write single coherent, forwardlooking description of what happens from the current state onward, as STEPBYSTEP CHAIN that follows the AGENT FUTURE exactly. The OUTPUT SHAPE is fixed: START with the OBSERVATION the PROPOSED NEXT ACTION produces the page state that results right after that action executes. THEN, for each subsequent step in the AGENT FUTURE, in order: the ACTION the actor takes and the OBSERVATION that action produces (action > resulting page state), chained one step after another. This reads as: proposedaction's result, then next action and its result, then the next, and so on one clause per step, following the real AGENT FUTURE turn by turn. Rules: FOLLOW THE GROUND TRUTH, STEP BY STEP: 18 describe the ACTUAL steps in the AGENT FUTURE, in their real order. Do NOT skip, merge, or reorder steps including routine navigation (clicking into menu/section, opening form, focusing field); each of these is its own step and gets its own clause. Do NOT jump ahead to later step's outcome, and do NOT invent steps that are not in the AGENT FUTURE. FAITHFUL TO THE OUTCOME: describe the ACTUAL path, not an idealized one. If the run SUCCEEDED, follow the route to the correct result and the actor terminating with the answer. If the run FAILED, describe honestly where it goes wrong the action that errors, the empty/wrong result it lands on, the loop it gets stuck in, or its terminating with an unverified/incorrect answer. Do NOT pretend failing run succeeds, and do NOT invent success it never reached. NO FUTURESPECIFIC VALUES: the summary is an ANTICIPATION of an unseen future, so it must not leak concrete values the current step could not yet know observed result names, counts, prices, dates, IDs, usernames, or the final answer. Refer to these by role and location ("you open the customer's profile", "the order total shown here is the answer"), never by literal value. value may be stated verbatim ONLY if it is already known now, i.e. it comes from the TASK OBJECTIVE or AGENT HISTORY. value the actor TYPES is not automatically allowed: if it was discovered earlier in the future, it is still futurespecific ("you search for the customer you found", not the literal name). Leaking such values trains the reader to hallucinate the contents of pages it has not seen. END CRITERION (WHERE TO STOP): The ask states WHERE the chain ends to how the task TERMINATES, after the next 5 steps, or up to the next milestone. Follow the AGENT FUTURE step by step until that end point and STOP there. Do not continue past it, and do not forecast steps beyond what the AGENT FUTURE shows. IMPORTANT: Address the actor in the second person ("You click ...", "the page now shows ..."). Describe both the actions and the resulting page states in plain natural language. Do NOT output literal browser actions, tool calls, JSON, semantic IDs, or code. OUTPUT FORMAT: Wrap your final summary in <summary> and </summary> tags, e.g. <summary>You click into the Reports menu and it expands to list the report categories. You choose Bestsellers, and the page loads report view with filter form above productranking table. You set the period dropdown to the year the objective asks about, and the form updates to expose the daterange fields. You click the From date field and it becomes focused. You type the start date into it, and the field now shows the entered date.</summary> User Prompt for Full-Traj & SubGoal-Traj Targets Generation on WebArena TASK OBJECTIVE: {task instruction} AGENT HISTORY (the actor's prior steps and the observation it currently faces, web pages omitted for brevity): {agent history} AGENT FUTURE (starting from the actor's decision at the current step, the steps this run actually took ground truth, not guess): {agent future} RUN OUTCOME: this trajectory ultimately {outcome}. {summary instruction} Summarize it as coherent forwardlooking anticipation in the second person, faithful to the RUN OUTCOME (if it failed, forecast the failure honestly; do not pretend it succeeds). FIRST, NOISE CHECK (do this before anything else): Compare the two runs step by step. If the FAILED RUN reaches essentially the SAME final page/state as the SUCCESSFUL RUN by essentially the same productive path and the ONLY meaningful difference is at the very LAST step (the terminate / answerreporting step), e.g. both read the same kind of result table but reported different final answer then no single action caused fixable pitfall; the failure is environmental (nondeterministic ordering, ties at topN cutoff, unstable data, an ambiguous reference answer). In that case output <pitfall>none</pitfall> and nothing else. YOUR JOB (when the NOISE CHECK does not trigger): 1. This is the single step where warning should have fired, and the step whose ACTION the world model would have been asked to verify. `fail_end_step` = the last step of the botched stretch (typically where the mistake's consequence became visible an empty result, an error, wrong termination). WRITE the PITFALL ANTICIPATION for the fail_start_step ACTION: few sentences predicting what goes wrong if the actor executes THAT proposed action the state or failure it leads to over the next steps (through roughly fail_end_step), and why. Write it as the world model's forecast of the consequence of taking that action, made from what is visible AT fail_start_step (before the bad outcome is revealed). HOW TO WRITE THE PITFALL ANTICIPATION: It is about the ACTION proposed at that step. Roll the environment forward from that action and describe the pitfall it produces ("executing this would land on an empty report because ...", "typing the date in this format would not be recognized, so the filter returns no records", "clicking here navigates away from the cart, losing the items added"). Forecast, do not command. Phrase it as prediction of consequences, NOT as an instruction ("set first", "click instead"). separate actor decides what to do about it. It must be ANTICIPATABLE from that step, not hindsight. When the trouble is something only discovered later (a tie at cutoff, an extra results page, validation error, an empty field, silent reset), state it as conditional consequence or general rule ("if the period is left as Day while the range spans month, the report tends to come back empty"), never as an asserted fact about specific contents. You have ground truth and may use it to understand the error, but do NOT bake specific counts, names, prices, or the final answer into the forecast. Ground it in the failed run's own state at that step. Keep it to few short sentences. Do NOT output literal browser actions, tool calls, semantic IDs, or code. OUTPUT FORMAT: Output ONE JSON object wrapped in <pitfall> and </pitfall>: {"fail_start_step": <int>, "fail_end_step": <int>, "pitfall_anticipation": "<a few sentences: the forecast of what the ACTION at fail_start_step leads to, as worldmodel prediction>"} fail_end_step must be >= fail_start_step. sections.title: System Prompt for PAWM on ScienceWorld
sections.content: You are ScienceWorld world model. separate "actor" agent actually plays the game; it has ALREADY chosen the single action it is about to take. Your job is to look at that PROPOSED action and mentally roll the environment forward not just the immediate next state, but the sequence of states and events likely to unfold AFTER it and, when the forecast is worth the actor's attention, tell it what the action leads to. This rollforward is your INTERNAL reasoning; you do not narrate it. You only SPEAK UP when the forecast is materially useful for the actor's next decision; otherwise you stay silent (emit <pass>). You are predictive model of the environment: you describe what would happen, you do not take actions yourself. The actor, which can see the full room, decides how to respond. ABOUT THE ENVIRONMENT AND ACTOR (a black box to you): ScienceWorld is text simulation of elementaryschool science experiments. The actor controls character in house of rooms (kitchen, bathroom, workshop, greenhouse, foundry, etc.) containing objects it can inspect and manipulate to complete scientific task. Each turn the actor takes ONE action from menu of currentlyvalid actions, e.g.: move between rooms (teleport/go/open door), pick up / put down / move objects, activate/deactivate devices (stove, freezer, blast furnace, sink), use thermometer, mix chemicals, read, wait (let time pass so heating/cooling/growth happens), and "focus on X". One mechanic worth knowing: `focus on X` is onetime, taskdefining commitment that marks as the target object; it is irreversible for the episode, so its consequences are worth forecasting carefully. You do NOT see the raw environment internals. You see the TASK, the actor's AGENT HISTORY (per prior turn: its thought, the 29 ACTION it took, and short observation), the CURRENT STATE (current room description + inventory + last observation), and most importantly the PROPOSED NEXT ACTION the actor is about to execute. YOUR JOB WORLDMODEL ROLLOUT OF THE PROPOSED ACTION: INTERNALLY (in your own reasoning, not in your output) roll the environment forward from the CURRENT STATE, starting with the PROPOSED NEXT ACTION: predict the state it produces, then the plausible states and events that follow over the next several steps as the actor continues toward the task goal. Reason about the trajectory this action commits the actor to, not just its immediate result. Then decide whether that forecast is worth surfacing. Do NOT write out the full rollout; it only determines whether you speak up. If the action is routine, expected step and the forecast is unremarkable, emit <pass> and nothing else. Speak up when the forecast is materially useful most importantly when the action would not advance the task the way the actor seems to expect (e.g. it produces no real state change, operates device whose precondition is not met, targets mislabeled object such as "tin cup" which is container made of tin rather than the substance "tin", commits irreversibly to the wrong target, repeats move that already made no progress, or ends/waits before the needed change has happened) but also when the forecast reveals something genuinely helpful for the actor to know before committing. Do NOT speak up merely because you would have chosen differently. When the action is reasonable and the outcome is ordinary, let it pass. When you do speak, describe concretely what the action would lead to the state or result it would most likely produce. Phrase it as prediction ("this would leave the cup empty because the sink has not been filled yet") rather than an instruction ("fill the cup first"). IMPORTANT: Do NOT output literal actions or object IDs. Give plain naturallanguage forecast. Keep it brief few short sentences describing the predicted outcome of this action, including the downstream consequence if it only surfaces few steps later. You are forecasting an outcome for the actor's consideration, not deciding for it. It is fine for the actor to proceed anyway. OUTPUT FORMAT: If the action is routine and the forecast is unremarkable, output single <pass> tag and nothing else no rollout, no explanation. The actor sees nothing in this case. Otherwise, output ONLY your forecast (not the full rollout that led you there) wrapped in <anticipation> and </anticipation> tags, e.g. <anticipation>Focusing on the tin cup here would commit the task's target to that object and end the episode: "tin cup" is container made of tin, not the pure substance "tin" the task refers to, so the outcome would be scored as the wrong target.</anticipation>

sections.title: System Prompt for PAWM on WebArena
sections.content: You are an expert webnavigation pitfall anticipation world model. separate "actor" agent actually drives the browser; it has ALREADY chosen the single action it is about to take. Your job is to look at that PROPOSED action and mentally roll the environment forward not just the immediate next state, but the sequence of states and events likely to unfold AFTER it to judge whether it leads into pitfall, now or downstream. This rollforward is your INTERNAL reasoning; you do not narrate it. You only SPEAK UP when that internal look reveals genuine pitfall and then you objectively preview just that pitfall. When the action looks sound, you stay silent (emit <pass>) and surface nothing to the actor. You are predictive model of the environment, NOT supervisor: you describe what could plausibly happen, you do NOT command the actor. You never take actions yourself, and you never tell the actor what to do you surface possible pitfall only when there is one, as neutral forecast, and leave it to the actor (who can see the full page) to judge whether the concern is warranted and how to respond. ABOUT THE ACTOR (a black box to you): The actor completes the objective by calling single tool, `step_browser`, once per turn. Each call performs one browser action and returns the resulting page state. `step_browser` can: click an element, type text into field (optionally pressing Enter), hover, select dropdown value, clear field, press key, navigate to URL, go back/forward, refresh, open/switch/close browser tab, and finally terminate the task while reporting an answer. You do NOT see the web pages. You see the actor's AGENT HISTORY (per prior turn: SUMMARIZATION of what it observed, its PLANNING, and the ACTION it took), the CURRENT BROWSER STATE, and most importantly the PROPOSED NEXT ACTION the actor is about to execute. YOUR JOB WORLDMODEL ROLLOUT OF THE PROPOSED ACTION: INTERNALLY (in your own reasoning, not in your output) roll the environment forward from the CURRENT BROWSER STATE, starting with the PROPOSED NEXT ACTION: predict the state it produces, then the plausible states and events that follow over the next several steps as the actor continues toward the objective. Reason about the trajectory this action commits the actor to, not just its immediate result. Then judge whether that unfolding leads to PITFALL either right away or downstream. Do NOT write out this rollout; it only determines whether you speak up. If it ends well, emit <pass> and nothing else; only if it reveals 30 pitfall do you externalize forecast (of that pitfall alone). pitfall need not be immediate: an action can look harmless this step yet steer the actor onto deadend path, wrong branch, or state that only reveals its problem several steps later (e.g. filling field that later step will silently reset, or entering flow that cannot reach the goal). Flag these downstream traps as well as immediate errors. Treat it as pitfall when the action is likely to: error out or be rejected; have no real effect / target the wrong or mislabeled element; enter data in wrong format or order so the result silently stays empty or wrong; navigate away from needed context or undo progress; repeat move that already failed or made no progress; or terminate/report an answer that has not actually been verified on the page. It is NOT pitfall when the action is sound, expected step that plausibly advances the objective even if it is not the only reasonable choice. Do NOT flag an action just because you would have picked different one; only flag genuine likely mistakes. When in doubt and the action is reasonable, let it pass. When you do surface pitfall, PREVIEW it objectively: describe concretely what could go wrong if the action plays out the state or failure it would likely lead to rather than issuing an instruction. Do NOT phrase it as command ("set first", "click instead"); phrase it as forecast of the consequence ("this would likely leave the report empty because ..."). The actor decides what, if anything, to do about it. IMPORTANT: Do NOT output literal browser actions, tool calls, semantic IDs, or code. Give plain naturallanguage preview of the possible pitfall. Keep it brief few short sentences, focused on the concrete pitfall this action could cause, including the downstream consequence if the risk only surfaces few steps later. Stay neutral and nondirective: you are anticipating possible outcome for the actor's consideration, not overriding its judgment. It is fine for the actor to proceed anyway if it judges the concern unwarranted. OUTPUT FORMAT: If the proposed action looks sound (no real pitfall worth previewing), stay silent: output single <pass> tag and nothing else no rollout, no explanation, no reassurance. The actor sees nothing in this case. If the proposed action could lead to pitfall, do NOT output <pass>; instead output ONLY your objective pitfall preview (not the full rollout that led you there) wrapped in <anticipation> and </anticipation> tags, e.g. <anticipation>If "Show Report" is clicked now, the report table would likely come back empty: the Period is still "Day" while the date range spans month, so the two are mismatched and the query tends to return no records.</anticipation>

sections.title: E RL Environment for WebArena
sections.content: Though WebArena (Zhou et al., 2024) provides its official environment for benchmark evaluation, we need to consider more when using the the environment for large scale interactions, such as during RL rollouts. The most significant problem for large scale interactions on the official WebArena environment is that the deployed WebArena docker for one website are shared for all tasks, where writing actions on the webpages (e.g., submitting PR in GitLab) would change the whole environment state and make them visible to all later tasks. Especially considering GRPO, running multiple examples within one group concurrently under the same docker will cause cross contamination. To solve this issue, the official WebArena suggests resetting the environment after each running of the whole benchmark, which requires removing all docker containers and then restarting them. This process normally takes minutes to complete, making it inefficient for huge throughput requirements. One recent work WebServ (Lu et al., 2025) proposes to uses Incus containers to create isolated containers for all written required tasks. Based on the paper, this will reduce launch latency by 5 and persistent storage by 240, enabling 200+ concurrent isolated environments on single host. Following this work, we therefore create Incus containers for all websites that require write actions, including Shopping, CMS, GitLab, and Reddit, leaving only the Map environment as the official one. Even after replicating WebServs setup for WebArena, however, we still find its stability fragile. Timeout errors occur frequently when requesting the websites at scale and considerable fraction of time is spent on environment retries when launching containers. As result, RL training on WebArena costs roughly twice as much as on ScienceWorld, which is why we did not run additional GRPO co-training for the baseline methods 31 on WebArena. Following WebServ, we implement an improved parser over raw HTML pages, which additionally constructs accessibility-tree-style observations with retained semantic IDs, reducing observation tokens by about half on average. We further find that WebArenas strictly rule-based evaluators, such as exact matching or substring-based matching, produce many false negatives, so we replace them with an LLM judge that issues the final binary reward. In addition, we apply hard truncation that limits each steps observation to 20k characters, which count roughly 5000 tokens.

sections.title: F Training Details for PAWM
sections.content: Here we present the training details of obtaining PAWM with both SFT and GRPO process. SFT. As in the pilot study experiments that train the world models, we again use LlamaFactory (Zheng et al., 2024) for SFT. We fine-tune Qwen3.5-27B on the synthetic pitfall dataset for 5 epochs, keeping the same hyperparameters as before: global batch size of 128 and learning rate of 2e-6 under cosine schedule with warmup ratio of 0.1. We cap the sequence length at 20480 tokens, and all training is performed on 16 NVIDIA B200 GPUs. GRPO Co-Training. Since the base black-box agent Claude Sonnet 4.5 is already capable with with high initial task accuracy, and we observe that many GRPO groups receive an identical reward of 1.0 across all rollouts, yielding zero advantage and thus no learning signal. This is even more prominent on WebArena-Lite, where the reward is binary. To improve RL effectiveness, we follow DAPO (Yu et al., 2026a) and adopt its dynamic sampling filter, which discards relative groups whose rollouts receive identical rewards. On WebArena-Lite, where accuracy already reaches 70% before training, discarding so many groups also slows DAPO training considerably. We therefore prefilter the training tasks before GRPO co-training by sampling each training task three times with the SFT PAWM and keeping only those that are not already solved in all three attempts. This finally results in 375 tasks as the training set for WebArena. We use Slime (Zhu et al., 2025) for GRPO co-training. Training for both benchmarks is initialized from the corresponding SFT PAWM and shares the same hyperparameters, which are listed in Table 7. All training is performed on 16 NVIDIA B200 GPUs.

sections.title: G Details of Baseline Methods
sections.content: Here we present the implementation details of the baseline methods compared in our main results. N/A. This is the vanilla setting, where the blackbox LLM agent performs the task on its own without any steering. RAG. RAG is simple yet effective promptbased steering method that requires no additional model to be trained. Specifically, we use Qwen3Embedding-0.6B to embed the task instructions and compute their cosine similarity. For each test instruction, we retrieve the most similar training instruction among those associated with successful trajectories. The retrieved trajectory is then inserted directly into the user prompt as context before the agent starts. Pre-Task Guidance. To construct the pre-task guidance dataset for SFT, we prompt Claude Sonnet 4.5 to read successful trajectory from the sampled dataset collected in our pilot study and write guidance for the specific task, mainly focusing on high-level planning.
